title: HAVING Clause vs WHERE Clause
description: Filter aggregated groups with HAVING, understand query execution order, and prevent common logical pitfalls.

data.text: A frequent interview question is the distinction between **`WHERE`** and **`HAVING`**. `WHERE` filters individual rows *before* grouping occurs. `HAVING` filters aggregated groups *after* the `GROUP BY` reduction has occurred.

data.caption: Logical Query Processing Order
data.definition:
flowchart LR
    A[1. FROM / JOIN] --> B[2. WHERE]
    B --> C[3. GROUP BY]
    C --> D[4. HAVING]
    D --> E[5. SELECT]
    E --> F[6. DISTINCT]
    F --> G[7. ORDER BY]
    G --> H[8. LIMIT / OFFSET]

data.title: Combining WHERE and HAVING in a Single Query
data.content: WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters aggregated totals.
data.code:
-- Find customers who placed more than 5 orders in 2024, with total spend > $1,000
SELECT 
    customer_id,
    COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
    SUM(total_amount) AS total_spend
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND created_at < '2025-01-01' -- WHERE: filters raw rows
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 AND SUM(total_amount) > 1000 -- HAVING: filters aggregated groups
ORDER BY total_spend DESC;

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: `WHERE` filters rows before grouping; `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation.
Never put row-level filters in `HAVING` because it prevents the planner from discarding unneeded rows early.
